MVC_App/Program.cs: Start here to see how the application is wired together. Telemetry is registered before the host is built, and both SQL contexts receive the command-logging interceptor. Cookies protect the browser pages; API controllers use the separate API-key scheme. Notice the middleware order: request logging sits outside the exception handlers so it can see the final result. Automatic API validation responses are suppressed so validation failures pass through the same error-handling path as other domain errors.
MVC_App/Telemetry/TelemetryExtensions.cs: This method connects the application's diagnostics to the Collector. It checks the endpoint and enable switch, adds service metadata, and registers logs, HTTP/SQL traces and runtime/server metrics. The SQL category filter reduces duplicate informational logs, while the enrichment callback puts command text on database spans. The numbered walkthrough after the code explains each registration and the limits worth keeping in mind.
MVC_App/Middleware/RequestLoggingMiddlew: Placing this middleware first lets it record the final response after the rest of the pipeline has run. It also handles exceptions that escape the inner handlers, without attaching the same exception twice if it was already logged. The completion event still matters even when another log describes the failure; that distinction is important when counting requests in Kibana.
MVC_App/Middleware/RequestLogging.cs: Rather than let every controller invent its own log format, this helper gives requests a common set of fields and severity rules: Information for 2xx/3xx, Warning for 4xx and Error for 5xx. It also tracks which exception was already logged. Pay attention to http.route_matched: the underscore prevents Elasticsearch from treating the existing http.route string as an object with a child field.
MVC_App/Middleware/ExceptionHandlingMidd: An API client needs an error response it can parse; a browser user needs a page. This middleware makes that choice, returning problem JSON for API calls and redirecting browser requests for known domain failures. Unexpected API exceptions become sanitized 500 responses, while unexpected browser exceptions go to the environment handler. This explains why a browser failure can have an error log followed by a 302 completion log.
MVC_App/Data/DbCommandLoggingInterceptor: The interceptor gives database calls a readable log alongside their trace spans. Its synchronous and asynchronous callbacks record the database, operation, duration and outcome, with command text limited to 1,000 characters in the message. Parameter values are not logged separately, but SQL literals still need a privacy review. Use the trace ID to connect these events to a request; a post-execution callback may run after the SQL Activity has stopped.
MVC_App/Authentication/ApiKeyAuthenticat: The API needs a 401 response when credentials are missing, not a redirect to an HTML login page. This handler reads the configured header, checks the allowed keys and returns JSON challenges or forbids. A valid key creates the caller's claims. The comparison is ordinal and the key represents an API client, not the browser user's delegated identity.
MVC_App/Diagnostics/ErrorConditions.cs: Stable category names make dashboard filters less fragile than message searches. This file maps status codes to those categories for both logs and problem responses. One useful detail: 503 maps to service_unavailable, so the server_error flag alone won't find every 5xx response.
MVC_App/Diagnostics/ApiProblemDetails.cs: When a call fails, this response gives the client a status, description and trace ID it can report back. The extra errorCategory and errorType fields make handling more predictable. WriteAsync uses application/problem+json and avoids rewriting a response that has already started.
MVC_App/Exceptions/AppExceptions.cs: These exception types give business failures an explicit meaning and HTTP status instead of treating every problem as a generic 500. The middleware uses them to build consistent responses and logs. DepartmentHasEmployeesException is particularly important: it protects a relationship that the database model does not express as a foreign key.
MVC_App/Controllers/Api/ApiControllerBas: The shared API behavior lives here: API-key authentication, explicit model validation and the simulate query option used for test failures. ThrowIfInvalid sends validation errors through the domain-exception path. Keep the fault-injection option restricted to a controlled environment; it is there to exercise the telemetry, not to serve normal clients.
MVC_App/Controllers/Api/DepartmentsApiCo: Department operations provide several useful paths to observe: a successful create, a duplicate name, a missing number and an attempted delete while employees still refer to the department. The controller applies those checks and uses CompanyContext for persistence. The surrounding instrumentation produces request spans, SQL spans and command logs without telemetry calls in every action.
MVC_App/Controllers/Api/EmployeesApiCont: The employee API supports CRUD and department filtering, checking that both the requested employee and any referenced department exist. DTOs keep its contract separate from the EF entities. These checks give the shared middleware concrete validation, conflict and not-found cases to report.
MVC_App/Controllers/Api/DiagnosticsApiCo: Use these endpoints when you want a known error without manipulating business rows. Ping works anonymously; whoami checks authentication; the remaining actions deliberately raise domain errors or an unhandled divide-by-zero. They are handy for validating a dashboard, but should not be exposed as an unrestricted production diagnostic surface.
MVC_App/Controllers/AccountController.cs: Registration and sign-in use the separate Identity database, so their SQL operations are observed too. Return URLs are checked before redirecting, and logout requires authentication and antiforgery validation. Those safeguards matter even though the focus of this sample is telemetry.
MVC_App/Controllers/DepartmentController: This is the browser-facing version of department CRUD, with cookie authorization and five-row pages. Missing records, duplicates and unsafe deletes become domain exceptions. Compare its failure path with the API controller: the browser can be redirected to an error page instead of receiving a JSON problem document.
MVC_App/Controllers/EmployeeController.c: The MVC employee screens get their data and department choices from this controller. Its paged CRUD and ListByDepartment actions share the same SQL instrumentation as the API, so you can investigate browser-driven database work with the same trace and log fields.
MVC_App/Models/CompanyContext.cs: CompanyContext maps the existing Department and Employee tables, including their keys, string lengths and unique department-name index. There is no employee-to-department foreign key configured here, which is why the controller checks matter. Program.cs supplies the connection and interceptor when it registers the context.
MVC_App/Models/Department.cs: The department entity is deliberately small: a number, name and location. The controller rules and CompanyContext mapping supply the behavior around those values.
MVC_App/Models/Employee.cs: This is the SQL Server employee shape used by the MVC application. Salary and employee details belong to business data; avoid copying them indiscriminately into log fields just because they are available on the entity.
MVC_App/Models/Api/ApiDtos.cs: The API exchanges these DTOs rather than exposing EF entities directly. Their annotations describe valid input, and the FromEntity/ToEntity methods keep the conversion explicit. Failed validation then follows the application's common error path.
MVC_App/Models/PaginatedList.cs: Pagination needs both the rows for the current page and a total count. CreateAsync performs those queries and calculates the navigation flags. When you inspect a page request, remember that this helper can account for more than one SQL command.
Extends IdentityUser without adding fields. It is the application's account type and remains separate from the business Employee entity.
IdentityDbContext<ApplicationUser> for the shared account database. Delegates model setup to Identity and is registered separately from CompanyContext.
MVC_App/ViewModels/LoginViewModel.cs: Models required email/password and the RememberMe choice for the MVC login form. Validation annotations drive server and unobtrusive browser validation; password fields must never be copied into telemetry.
MVC_App/ViewModels/RegisterViewModel.cs: Models registration email, password length and matching confirmation. Compare validation prevents mismatched passwords before Identity account creation.
MVC_App/Migrations/Identity/202610010802: Initial code-first Identity migration. Up creates user, role, claim, login, token and join tables, their keys, foreign keys and indexes; Down removes the schema in dependency-safe order. This migration belongs to the account database, not the database-first Company schema.

EF-generated target model associated with the initial Identity migration. BuildTargetModel preserves the model metadata used when that migration was created; it is not request-processing code and emits no application telemetry by itself.
MVC_App/Migrations/Identity/IdentityCont: EF-generated current Identity model snapshot. Future migrations compare the configured model against this baseline. Included because it is source-controlled code, although it is not an exporter or middleware component.
MVC_App/Pages/Error.cshtml.cs: The error page reads the supplied status and message, disables caching and shows an Activity-based or HTTP request identifier. If the browser arrived through a redirect, that identifier may belong to the new request. Look back to the original error event when you need the failing request's trace.
MVC_App/Pages/Index.cshtml.cs: The home page has an empty OnGet handler, which makes it a simple way to check the web host. Request instrumentation still observes the visit even though the page doesn't write a custom log.
MVC_App/Pages/Privacy.cshtml.cs: This page model keeps the template's empty OnGet handler and injected logger. Like the home page, it lets you exercise the HTTP pipeline without a business-data query.
MVC_App/Pages/Error.cshtml: The page displays the status, message and request identifier. Razor encodes normal expressions, but that doesn't decide whether an error message is appropriate to share. Review detailed business errors before showing them publicly.
MVC_App/Pages/Index.cshtml: The welcome page is useful as a first smoke check because it doesn't depend on the Company database. A successful visit tells you the host is serving pages, not that every dependency is healthy.
MVC_App/Pages/Privacy.cshtml: This is the template's privacy-policy placeholder. A deployed application needs a real policy that also covers its telemetry collection and retention.
MVC_App/Pages/Shared/_Layout.cshtml: Razor Pages and MVC views share this navigation and page shell. It brings in Bootstrap, jQuery, the site assets and any page-specific Scripts section, and changes the account controls according to sign-in state.
MVC_App/Pages/Shared/_Layout.cshtml.css: These scoped rules keep the shared navigation, buttons and footer consistent across the browser screens.
MVC_App/Pages/Shared/_ValidationScriptsP: Loads jQuery Validate and its unobtrusive adapter. Browser validation improves feedback but does not replace server-side validation or the API's error mapping.
MVC_App/Pages/_ViewImports.cshtml: Supplies Razor Pages namespace/usings and MVC tag helpers used by page markup.
MVC_App/Pages/_ViewStart.cshtml: Chooses _Layout as the default Razor Pages layout.
MVC_App/Views/_ViewImports.cshtml: Imports application/model namespaces and MVC tag helpers for MVC view compilation.
MVC_App/Views/_ViewStart.cshtml: Points MVC views at /Pages/Shared/_Layout.cshtml, unifying page and MVC navigation.
MVC_App/Views/Account/AccessDenied.cshtm: Displays a simple access-denied message and login link; authorization enforcement lives in the server pipeline, not in this markup.
MVC_App/Views/Account/Login.cshtml: Strongly typed login form with validation, RememberMe and a return URL. Password input is masked in the UI and is not a suitable telemetry field.
MVC_App/Views/Account/Register.cshtml: Registration form containing email, password and confirmation with validation feedback. Submission reaches the Identity-backed AccountController.
MVC_App/Views/Department/Index.cshtml: The department table links to each CRUD action and to the employees in a selected department. Its previous/next controls are a convenient way to observe the paging queries behind a normal browser request.
MVC_App/Views/Department/Create.cshtml: The form collects the department number, name and location. Client validation gives quick feedback, but the controller and database still decide whether the number and name are unique.
MVC_App/Views/Department/Edit.cshtml: The department number stays read-only while the user edits the name and location. The server must still validate the submitted values; a read-only input is a UI choice, not an authorization rule.
MVC_App/Views/Department/Details.cshtml: After the controller finds a department, this view displays its fields with edit and back navigation. A missing record takes the error path before the view can render.
MVC_App/Views/Department/Delete.cshtml: The confirmation form posts the department number back to the controller. The important business check—whether employees still use that department—happens on the server.
MVC_App/Views/Employee/Index.cshtml: This table is the starting point for the MVC employee screens. Paging, CRUD links and department filtering give you several ordinary browser actions to compare in the request logs.
MVC_App/Views/Employee/Create.cshtml: The create form gets its department choices from ViewBag.Departments, so users can select a known name rather than type one. Validation messages appear beside the submitted fields.
MVC_App/Views/Employee/Edit.cshtml: Notice the difference from the create form: DeptName is a text input here, while EmpNo is read-only. That makes the server's department validation especially important when an update is submitted.
MVC_App/Views/Employee/Details.cshtml: A read-only view of the selected employee, with links back to the list or into the edit screen. The controller has already done the lookup by the time this renders.
MVC_App/Views/Employee/Delete.cshtml: The page asks for confirmation and posts the hidden employee key. The delete itself belongs to the controller's POST action, not to rendering this page.
The GET form filters the table by department and shows which choice is active. Use it when you want repeatable read traffic through MVC rather than through the JSON API.
MVC_App/wwwroot/css/site.css: The shared site stylesheet supplies the template's responsive sizing, focus styles and page layout. Requests for the asset also pass through the outer request logger.
MVC_App/wwwroot/js/site.js: This template file contains comments but no custom JavaScript. The application telemetry comes from the server-side setup, not from a browser SDK loaded here.
MVC_App/Dockerfile: The optional container build publishes with the .NET 10 SDK, then runs MVC_App.dll in an ASP.NET runtime image as APP_UID on port 8080. Compose does not start this image. If you choose to use it, provide its database and telemetry configuration separately.
MVC_App/MVC_App.csproj: Web SDK project targeting net10.0. References EF Core SQL Server/tools/design, Identity and OpenTelemetry hosting/OTLP/ASP.NET Core/HttpClient/runtime/SqlClient packages. The exact versions below are the workspace snapshot, not an instruction to upgrade packages.
MVC_App/appsettings.json: The base settings bring together logging levels, allowed hosts, both SQL connections and the API-key configuration. Supply private values for the redacted entries. The OTLP endpoint comes from the development settings or environment rather than this file.
MVC_App/appsettings.Development.json: These overrides enable detailed errors and point the web app at the local Collector with its own service name. One setting deserves care: the SDK does not necessarily read OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL from JSON. Set it in the process environment unless you've added explicit options binding.
MVC_App/Properties/launchSettings.json: Local launch profiles for HTTP/HTTPS and IIS Express, including Development environment and URLs. These settings are used by tooling, not automatically by a published production process.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Program.cs: The Blazor host combines interactive-server components, the shared account database and a typed client for the MVC API. Its own cookie keeps the two web sessions separate. Request logging wraps the pipeline, while the HTTP handler and error-boundary logger cover outgoing calls and component failures. The development-only certificate bypass is worth noticing before you reuse this configuration elsewhere.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Telemetry/Telemetry: Blazor sends its logs, HTTP traces and runtime/HTTP metrics to the same Collector as MVC_App, but uses a distinct service name. That lets you search both services together or separate them in Kibana. Unlike the MVC extension, this one does not add SqlClient instrumentation for its direct Identity database calls.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Telemetry/AppLoggin: Keeping the status and error fields consistent with MVC means the same queries can work for both applications. This helper adds the Blazor component label, lets callers supply their own context and drops null fields such as a missing exception type.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Telemetry/ApiLoggin: An HTTP span won't appear in the log index by itself. This handler therefore writes a structured log for each typed-client API call, including its duration. Transport exceptions are classified as 503 and rethrown; the catch also includes cancellation paths. These records complement the separate HttpClient spans.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Telemetry/RequestLo: The Blazor host records its incoming HTTP outcomes here, but skips /_blazor circuit traffic to avoid a noisy log stream. For failures inside a later component event, look to the error boundary or the outgoing API handler rather than expecting this middleware to describe every click.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Telemetry/LoggingEr: When a component failure reaches ErrorBoundary, this logger gives it the same searchable fields as an API error. An ApiException keeps its original status instead of becoming a blanket 500. Errors already caught and handled by a page don't reach this boundary.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Api/ApiDtos.cs: These local DTOs mirror the backend's department, employee and problem-response contracts. They make typed calls straightforward, but there is no shared contract assembly to keep the two copies synchronized automatically.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Api/ApiException.cs: ApiException carries the failed status, parsed problem, category and server trace ID together. Components can give the user a useful message and a diagnostic reference without exposing a stack trace.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Api/MvcAppApiClient: The component code doesn't need to repeat JSON serialization and problem-response handling for every operation. This typed client does that work and raises ApiException on failure. It also treats an unexpectedly empty success body as a problem when the caller expects a value.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Diagnostics/ErrorCo: The client uses the same status-to-category vocabulary as the server. Keep the two definitions aligned when adding a new error case; otherwise a shared dashboard filter can quietly miss one side of the call.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Identity/IdentityMo: Defines this project's Identity user/context mapping for the existing MVC_AppIdentity database. It shares accounts, not cookies or automatic single sign-on, and does not own migrations.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Identity/AuthEventL: Writes structured sign-in/sign-out outcomes and coarse failure reasons. It does not log the password, but does log the user name, which still requires a personal-data and retention review.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Components/App.razo: The application shell loads the assets and Blazor scripts and chooses the render mode. Most pages become interactive on the server, while excluded account pages stay on the normal HTTP path so sign-in and sign-out can change cookies.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Components/Routes.r: AuthorizeRouteView chooses the page according to the user's authentication state, redirecting anonymous visitors to sign in. This controls access to the UI; the backend still checks the API credential independently.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Components/_Imports: Shared Razor component usings for routing, authorization, forms, rendering and application types.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Components/Layout/M: Alongside the navigation and account controls, the layout wraps page content in an ErrorBoundary. It can show diagnostic information and let the user recover after a component failure. That matters in Blazor because the original page request may be long finished when a later event throws.
These scoped rules control how the Blazor error notification appears within the layout.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Components/Layout/R: When the interactive circuit disconnects, this dialog tells the user whether reconnection is in progress or needs another attempt. Its module hook connects the markup to the retry logic.
The dialog's visibility and animation change with the reconnect state. These rules make a transport interruption understandable to the user while the application attempts recovery.

The module attempts to reconnect or resume the circuit and updates the retry UI. If the server rejects recovery, it reloads the page. This handles the browser experience during an interruption; server telemetry is still needed to investigate the cause.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Components/Account/: Sign-in stays on the static-server-rendered path so Identity can set the authentication cookie. The form checks local return URLs, reports a generic failure and logs the outcome. The current flow does not enable lockout on failure, which is worth revisiting for production use.
Signing out also needs an HTTP response to clear the cookie. This POST-based page clears the session, logs the action and redirects the browser.
An anonymous visitor is sent to sign-in with a return URL, so the application can bring them back to the page they originally requested.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Components/Pages/Ho: The home page introduces the sample's logging paths and trace correlation before the user starts exercising the CRUD and diagnostic screens.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Components/Pages/De: The department grid uses the typed API client for its CRUD operations. Expected API errors are caught and displayed in place; unexpected exceptions can reach the layout boundary. Follow the outgoing call log and backend trace to see what happened beyond the component.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Components/Pages/Em: This grid loads department choices as well as employee data, so one screen action can result in several API calls. It displays known API failures inline and leaves unexpected exceptions to the boundary. That distinction explains why not every failed call produces a component-boundary log.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Components/Pages/Di: The diagnostic buttons let you compare a handled API failure, an uncaught component error and an unreachable endpoint. The unreachable case creates a separate HttpClient, bypassing ApiLoggingHandler. Keep that detail in mind if you can't find the handler's usual structured event for that call.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Components/Pages/Er: The error page shows the available Activity or HTTP request identifier. Use it as a starting point for investigation, while remembering that a later circuit event may not share the original page request's trace.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Components/Pages/No: The missing-route screen gives the user a clear destination when navigation cannot find a page.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Components/Shared/A: This dismissible alert keeps API failures consistent across the CRUD screens. Showing the category and server trace ID gives a user something useful to report without displaying the whole exception.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/wwwroot/app.css: Global styles for application layout, CRUD grids, forms, alerts and authentication pages. No telemetry scripts are embedded in this stylesheet.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/MVC_App.BlazorClien: net10.0 Web SDK project with Identity/EF SQL Server and OTel HTTP/runtime/OTLP dependencies. Interactive-server components run in this server process; this is not a WebAssembly telemetry exporter.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/appsettings.json: These settings tell Blazor where to find the API, which header/key to send and which Identity database to use. Replace the redacted connection values privately before running it.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/appsettings.Develop: The development settings point to the local API and Collector. Keep the Blazor service name distinct from MVC_App so shared-index searches can separate them. Set SDK export-interval options in the process environment when you want to control their effect.
MVC_App.BlazorClient/Properties/launchSe: The Blazor launch profiles bind HTTP on 5072 and HTTPS on 7213 in Development. These are the UI addresses, not the MVC API addresses configured in its typed client.
MVC_App.ApiClient/Program.cs: The console starts by choosing a scenario or load run, then sets up cancellation and the API wrapper. It masks the credential in its display and uses exit codes to report the outcome. The telemetry to inspect is produced by the backend; this executable does not register OTel providers.
MVC_App.ApiClient/ClientOptions.cs: Use these options to choose the API address, key, iteration count, delays and load concurrency. Environment variables can supply the URL/key without putting credentials in command-line arguments. The defaults target MVC's HTTPS development profile; the insecure TLS option should stay limited to local testing.
MVC_App.ApiClient/MvcAppApiClient.cs: A deliberate 409 or 500 is a test result, not a reason to stop the whole run. This wrapper returns ApiCallResult for HTTP and transport failures and applies a 30-second timeout, allowing the reporting code to compare the outcomes consistently.
MVC_App.ApiClient/ApiCallResult.cs: Each result holds the status and elapsed time together with any problem-response metadata. In particular, the returned traceId gives you a direct starting point for finding the backend events behind a console failure.
MVC_App.ApiClient/ScenarioRunner.cs: The scenario walks through successful CRUD and known failure cases, then attempts cleanup. Validation errors, missing records, conflicts and simulated dependency failures are intentional here. Keep that test traffic separate from a dashboard meant to measure normal availability.
MVC_App.ApiClient/ConsoleReport.cs: This report puts the per-call results and final summary in a readable console format, including diagnostic fields on failures. It stays local; there is no exporter forwarding these console lines to ELK.
MVC_App.ApiClient/LoadPlan.cs: Before starting workers, the plan groups dependent operations into lifecycle units so creates, updates and deletes can run in a sensible order while meeting the requested verb counts. Generated IDs start in the 500000 range. Use an isolated database to avoid collisions with existing data.
MVC_App.ApiClient/LoadRunner.cs: A bounded worker pool executes the plan, reports progress and responds to cancellation. Failed operations are not retried, which helps keep the reported attempts aligned with the workload you requested.
MVC_App.ApiClient/LoadStats.cs: Each worker collects counts and timing samples before the results are merged. Percentiles use the nearest-rank method. These numbers describe the client's observed call time, not just server execution, and are separate from the backend's OTel metrics.
MVC_App.ApiClient/LoadReport.cs: The load report summarizes status counts, throughput and latency. Check LoadPlan rather than relying on the report's hard-coded ID-range message when deciding which rows belong to a run; the displayed range can differ from the generated one.
MVC_App.ApiClient/MVC_App.ApiClient.cspr: Minimal net10.0 console executable with no package references. In particular it has no OpenTelemetry SDK/exporter dependency; server-side traces still exist for requests it generates.
MVC_App.PgSqlClient/Program.cs: This console needs a little more startup and shutdown work than the API traffic generator. It builds a generic host, registers Azure Monitor telemetry and a pooled NpgsqlDataSource, then runs the selected workload. Npgsql uses the shared logger factory with parameter logging disabled. The final flush is important: a short run can finish before the next scheduled export.
MVC_App.PgSqlClient/ClientOptions.cs: Configuration and command-line options control the database, workload and export settings. Connection descriptions mask the password, but the default SslMode.Require only encrypts the connection; use VerifyFull with trusted certificates when you need peer validation. The metric interval option changes the optional console reader, not Azure Monitor's minute-scale reader.
MVC_App.PgSqlClient/Telemetry/TelemetryB: Here the same three signals go to a different backend. Business activities, Npgsql spans, application logs and custom/runtime/process metrics feed Azure Monitor when a connection string is configured. Optional console exporters help inspect the signals locally. Notice the employee-duration buckets through 10,000 ms and the explicit shutdown flush; there is no Collector exporter in this setup.
MVC_App.PgSqlClient/Telemetry/AppDiagnos: Runtime metrics can tell you about the process, but these instruments tell you about the work: employee operations, rows read or changed, failures and duration. The observable gauges expose the latest table snapshot, including active-row and salary totals. They are refreshed by snapshot queries rather than continuously polling PostgreSQL.
MVC_App.PgSqlClient/Data/EmployeeReposit: ExecuteAsync wraps the parameterized database operations in a common observation path. It records timing and counts, marks failed spans with exception/SQLSTATE information, logs and rethrows failures, and updates gauges after snapshot queries. Npgsql adds lower-level command spans beneath these business operations, giving you both an application-level and a database-level view.
MVC_App.PgSqlClient/Data/Employee.cs: The PostgreSQL sample has its own Employee shape, display formatting and snapshot/department-summary records. Don't confuse it with the differently shaped SQL Server entity used by MVC_App.
MVC_App.PgSqlClient/EmployeeWorkload.cs: A scenario activity surrounds the reads, writes, soft deletes, summaries and cleanup. Optional duplicate-email and missing-ID failures give you recognizable error cases, including PostgreSQL SQLSTATE 23505. Start with read-only mode against a training database before enabling the mutation phases.
MVC_App.PgSqlClient/InteractiveSession.c: The interactive loop creates an activity for each command and catches failures so one bad operation need not end the session. When you exit, it returns to Program.cs and its final telemetry flush rather than abandoning the last batch.
net10.0 executable referencing Azure Monitor OTel exporter, generic hosting, Npgsql and Npgsql.OpenTelemetry, plus runtime/process/console instrumentation. Copies appsettings.json to output and declares a user-secrets ID. The dependency list confirms its destination is Azure Monitor, not ELK.
MVC_App.PgSqlClient/appsettings.json: Supplies PostgreSQL connection fields, Azure Monitor connection information and logging levels. The original workspace contains sensitive values; this publication replaces them. Connection credentials and monitoring identifiers should be provisioned privately instead of copied into a public blog.
MVC_App.PgSqlClient/README.md: Project-specific runbook covering options, database prerequisites, telemetry, final flush and Azure Monitor queries. It is included as supporting documentation, not executable code. Azure's Kusto Query Language examples are not interchangeable with Kibana Query Language despite both being abbreviated KQL.
compose.yaml: Runs Elasticsearch and Kibana 9.5.4, Collector Contrib 0.161.0 and Logstash 9.5.4 on a telemetry bridge network. Publishes only loopback 9200/5601/4318. Mounts Collector configuration, shared log files and Logstash pipeline, and persists Logstash read offsets in logstash-data. Applications/databases are not services in this Compose file. Elasticsearch has no explicitly managed named data volume here.
observability/otel-collector.yaml: Accepts OTLP/HTTP on 4318. Memory limiter and batch processor precede every exporter. Traces/metrics go directly to Elasticsearch's OTel-compatible data streams; logs go to a rotating JSONL file for Logstash. The Elasticsearch queue/retry settings do not make a durable disk-backed trace/metric spool.
observability/logstash/pipeline/otel-log: Tails split JSON lines with the json codec and persistent sincedb offsets. Ruby decodes OTLP AnyValue, traverses resourceLogs/scopeLogs/logRecords and emits one small event per record, avoiding nested-split copying costs. Normalizes legacy http.route.matched, copies resource/scope/trace fields, converts timestamps, cancels the wrapper and indexes mvcapp-logs-YYYY.MM.dd.
scripts/test-telemetry.py: Standard-library host-side smoke test starts a temporary OTLP HTTP receiver and the built MVC server on temporary ports. Checks nonempty protobuf exports with service identity for logs/traces/metrics, then disabled/unconfigured cases and five non-destructive routes. It checks receipt, not complete protobuf semantics, Elasticsearch mappings or a running ELK stack.
.dockerignore: Excludes build outputs, IDE state, secrets/certificates, appsettings, local launch settings and support folders from the Docker context. Since appsettings files are excluded, a containerized web app needs external configuration; the Dockerfile alone is not a complete runnable deployment.
MVC_App.sln: Visual Studio solution linking all four net10.0 projects and their build configurations. It establishes documentation coverage; it does not start the Collector or deploy databases.
